newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania goes to polls, Landsbergis votes early.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania goes to polls, Landsbergis votes early.

text.p: Lithuania began voting on Sunday in its second parliamentary elections since quitting the former Soviet Union and opinion polls suggested independence hero Vytautas Landsbergis could return to power.
Polling stations opened at seven a.m. (0400 GMT) and were due to close at nine p.m. (1800 GMT) in the first round of the elections. A run-off has been set for November 10.
Landsbergis, one of the first to vote, is leading his Homeland Union in a bid to unseat his bitter foes, the ex-Communists of the ruling Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP).
He told reporters he was voting for a "clean pair of hands", a reference to the many accusations of corruption he has made against the LDLP.
"I am voting for improvement and that means stability," he added.
The former music professor was an unlikely hero when he led the Baltic state of 3.6 million people to independence from Moscow.

Landsbergis and his people won the admiration of the world by standing up to Soviet might, especially after a hardline crackdown in January 1991 in which 13 people were killed during an assault on the television tower in the capital Vilnius.
His political movement was dumped in general elections in 1992 as Lithuania's economy collapsed, inflation soared and his party was riven by internal bickering.
In a vote that set a trend in Eastern Europe, Lithuanians propelled the former Communists of the LDLP back into power.
The LDLP's victory was firmly sealed the following year when party leader Algirdas Brazauskas was elected president.
Opinion polls show the Homeland Union has a good chance of becoming the largest party in parliament but that it is likely to have to form a coalition in the 141-seat chamber to displace the LDLP.
The LDLP has made economic gains and been applauded by the International Monetary Fund despite winning power on a populist platform of easing the pain of reforms.
But many people are disillusioned with the party and have criticised it for corruption.
It was badly discredited by a banking crisis at the end of last year when a former prime minister withdrew his personal savings from a bank days before it was shut.
The Homeland Union has said it will work with the Christian Democrats but it is not certain which other parties it can strike a deal with.

Political commentators say Lithuanians, tired of the battle between Landsbergis and the LDLP and disillusioned with politics, may choose a "third force" or register a protest vote by backing fringe groups.
